title: Why files? Data that survives after the program ends

visuals.title: The life of a file operation: open, check, use, close

stages.name: 1. Open
stages.detail: Create a stream object (ofstream to write, ifstream to read) and give it the file name: ofstream out("data.txt");

stages.name: 2. Check
stages.detail: Ask if the file really opened: if (!out). A file can fail to open (missing file, wrong folder, no permission).

stages.name: 3. Read / write
stages.detail: Use << to put data into the file or >> and getline to take data out of it, exactly like cout and cin.

stages.name: 4. Close
stages.detail: Call out.close(). All data is saved and the file is free for other programs.

visuals.title: Match each file idea to its meaning

pairs.meaning: Output file stream: writes data INTO a file (like cout)
Input file stream: reads data FROM a file (like cin)
One stream that can read and write
The header that gives you all the file streams
Open for append: keep the old content, add at the end
Check that the file opened correctly
Finish with the file and save everything

goal: After this you can explain why programs need files, name the three file streams, and follow the open, check, use, close steps for any file task.
warmup: Think of your mobile phone contacts. When you switch the phone off, the numbers are still there tomorrow. That is because they are saved in the phone's storage. Now think of a number you only remember in your head while you search for a pen: if somebody distracts you, it is gone. A normal C++ variable is like the number in your head. When the program ends, it is gone. A file is like the saved contact list.
definition: A file is a named place on the disk (for example marks.txt) where data is stored permanently. Variables live in RAM, which is temporary, so everything in them is lost when the program ends, and anything typed with the keyboard has to be typed again at the next run. A text file stores data as readable characters: you can open it in Notepad. (A binary file stores the raw bytes of the data instead and is not readable in Notepad; in this course we use text files only.) In C++ you work with a file through a stream, an object that carries data to or from the file. The header <fstream> gives you three stream types: ofstream (output, writes to a file, like cout), ifstream (input, reads from a file, like cin) and fstream (can do both).
howItWorks: Every file task follows the same steps. (1) #include <fstream>. (2) Create a stream object and give it the file name, for example ofstream out("data.txt"); this also opens the file. (3) Check that it opened with if (!out). (4) Use << (writing) or >> and getline (reading). (5) Close the file with out.close(). Watch the trace: the first stream creates names.txt and writes Ali, the second opens the SAME file with ios::app and adds Sana, the third reads it back. The file name is a relative path: the program looks for it in its working folder, which is the folder where the program is run. A name like "data.txt" means "in my own folder". Do not write a full path such as C:\\Users\\Ali\\data.txt, because it will not exist on another computer. When you write with ofstream and the file already exists, its old content is erased. To keep the old content and add new text at the end, open the file with ios::app. In the examples of this week every program writes a file first and then reads it back, so you can see the result without any other tool.

sample.title: Write, append, read back

explanation.text: Opens names.txt for writing. Any old content would be erased.
First line of the file.
ios::app = append. The old content (Ali) is kept and new output goes after it.
Second line of the file.
Opens the file for reading from the beginning.
Counts the lines that we read.
Reads one line each time. When there are no more lines the read fails and the loop stops by itself.

steps.note: The program creates the stream object out and opens names.txt for writing. The file did not exist, so it is created empty.
out works like cout, but the text goes into the file, not the screen.
The first stream is closed. Ali is safely saved on the disk.
The file is opened again, this time with ios::app (append). The old content Ali is KEPT and new text will go after it.
Sana is added at the end of the file (shown here as lines separated by |).
Now an input stream in opens the same file for reading, starting from the first line.
count will count the lines we read.
getline reads the first line into line.
One line was read, so count becomes 1.
The line is shown on the screen with its number.
The loop condition failed at the end of the file, so the loop stopped. Now the file is closed.

variations.when: Writing. Creates the file or ERASES the old content.
Appending. Keeps the old content and adds at the end.
Reading. The file must already exist.
One kind of object for reading or writing; the mode says which.
Always, when you finish with the file.
Right after opening, to catch a missing file or wrong folder.

mistakes.error: The compiler reports error: variable 'std::ofstream out' has initializer but incomplete type. The file streams live in <fstream>, so you must include it.
The compiler reports error: no match for 'operator>>' (operand types are 'std::ofstream' {aka 'std::basic_ofstream<char>'} and 'int'). An ofstream can only write. To read you need an ifstream.

mistakes.wrong:
ofstream out("scores.txt");   // run again later to add a score
out << 55 << endl;
mistakes.error: No compiler error. Plain ofstream erases the old content every time the program runs, so earlier scores disappear. Use ios::app to keep them.
No compiler error. If data.txt is missing or in another folder, the read quietly fails and x holds a useless value. Always check right after opening.
No compiler error. The long path only works on one computer. Use a plain file name and keep the file in the program's working folder.

examTips: Learn the steps in order: include <fstream>, create the stream, open, check, read/write, close. Exams often ask you to list them.
ofstream = output (write), ifstream = input (read), fstream = both. A common 1-mark question.
Plain ofstream erases old content. If the question says "add" or "keep the previous records", the answer needs ios::app.
Write if (!out) or if (!in) right after opening. Examiners give marks for the check.
Say the reason for files: RAM is temporary, a file is permanent.
romanSummary: Variable ka data RAM mein hota hai, program band hote hi khatam ho jata hai. File mein data disk par permanent rehta hai.
<fstream> include karein: ofstream likhne ke liye, ifstream parhne ke liye, fstream dono ke liye.
Steps: stream banao, file kholo, check karo (if (!out)), parho ya likho, aakhir mein close() karo.
ofstream purana data mita deta hai; purana data rakhna ho to ios::app use karein.
File ka naam sirf "data.txt" likhein, poora path nahi, program usi folder mein dhoondta hai jahan woh chal raha hai.
